lesson.title: Learned DBMS components: predictions need a systems contract
lesson.short: Cardinality · plan ranking · learned indexes · robust evaluation
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: A model can reduce prediction error and still make a database slower. Follow the decision from features to plan to measured execution.
goals: Locate learning at cardinality estimation, cost/ranking, indexing and configuration boundaries.
Calculate q-error and end-to-end break-even cost.
Design a leakage-resistant evaluation with a safe conventional fallback.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
A query used to finish in 82 ms. After adding a model it finishes in 69 ms. That sounds useful. But if the next query changes from 5 ms to 11 ms, should the same model still be used? This lesson follows one decision all the way from a predicted row count to the time the user waits.

You need the idea that different correct query plans can have different costs from lessons 17–18. No model training is needed for the paper exercises. All numerical examples here are original teaching examples.

This is an original supplemental companion, not an Edinburgh lecture or a verified Canvas assignment. Activities and suggested time are practice guidance. Assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Four places to introduce learning
sections.html:
Imagine counting customers before choosing a join. If we expect 500 rows, we may choose a small in-memory strategy; 5,000 actual rows can change its cost. A model that predicts this count is a cardinality estimator. Its output helps a decision; it does not replace the actual query result.

Now suppose all candidate plans are already known. Predicting their costs or ranking them is a different task: a plan ranker chooses a plan. A third task, a learned index, predicts a key's position. A fourth, a configuration advisor, suggests memory settings, indexes or other resource choices for the workload. These are different inputs and outputs, so a good model for one is not automatically suitable for another.

Follow an original lookup: prediction → position 420; valid error bound → 6; candidate positions → 414 through 426 inclusive; search these positions → compare the actual keys; return the verified match. Returning the item at 420 without comparison would turn a performance error into a wrong answer. A bound seen only on training keys is not a bound for future keys. Inserts, deletes and changed distributions need an updated correct search procedure or fallback.

For each component, write its input, permitted output, correctness check, update policy and fallback. Row-count errors normally change performance; unchecked position errors can change answers. Configuration errors can affect concurrent queries as well. This is why the systems contract comes before the choice of neural network.

Key takeaway

A learned component is useful only inside a complete algorithm that preserves correctness and accounts for prediction, maintenance and fallback cost.

sections.title: Worked example: correlation and q-error
sections.html:
Use one Customer snapshot with 100,000 rows. First count City A: 10% means 10,000 rows. Next count commuter-pass holders: 5% means 5,000 rows. Finally ask for both conditions. The key fact is that every pass holder lives in City A, so all 5,000 survive the conjunction.

What would an independence assumption do? It takes the 10,000 City A rows and keeps 5% of them: 10,000 × 0.05 = 500. The assumption treats pass ownership as equally common inside and outside City A, which contradicts the stated data. We can now name the problem: correlated attributes defeat this independence estimate.

To compare positive counts c and estimates ĉ, compute both ratios and take the larger: q-error = max(ĉ/c, c/ĉ). At ĉ=500 and c=5,000, the ratios are 0.1 and 10, giving 10. At ĉ=4,000, they are 0.8 and 1.25, giving 1.25. The metric is always at least one. With zeros, division fails, so report a convention such as replacing each value by max(value,1).

Why still measure execution? The smaller error might occur at a harmless subplan, while another error crosses a memory threshold and causes spilling. Keep the plan, memory use and runtime beside q-error.

Try a new case: estimate 60,000, actual 15,000. Then reverse the two. What changes?

Both have q-error 4: max(4,0.25)=4. The metric is symmetric, but the system cost need not be. Allocating too much memory and spilling after allocating too little are different consequences.

sections.title: Prediction quality versus end-to-end benefit
sections.html:
Return to the query the user waits for. The conventional path spends 2 ms planning and 80 ms executing: 2+80=82 ms. The learned path spends 9 ms planning and 60 ms executing: 9+60=69 ms. It saves 13 ms end to end. The speedup is 82/69≈1.19; using 80/60≈1.33 silently removes planning from the question.

Try the same selectors on a shorter query. Conventional execution is 3 ms, giving 2+3=5 ms. Learned execution is 2 ms, giving 9+2=11 ms. Saving 1 ms of execution cannot pay for 7 ms of extra planning. A fallback can therefore be useful even when every chosen plan is legal.

Training and label collection also consume resources. With a one-time cost of 1,800 seconds and a saving of 0.013 seconds per request, n requests break even when 0.013n≥1,800. Thus n≥138,462 whole requests in this simplified model. Retraining and operating costs raise the requirement; report the amortization assumption rather than hiding it.

To diagnose selection, measure the fastest plan among the same supplied candidates after running them. This candidate-plan oracle uses hindsight and is a diagnostic reference, not a deployable selector or proof of global optimality.

Candidate oracle 40 ms, learned choice 60 ms, native choice 100 ms: what should be improved?

The 20 ms learned-to-oracle execution gap suggests ranking headroom. The 40 ms native-to-learned saving still needs planning overhead added. Even the oracle may miss a better plan that was never proposed. Report workload totals, per-query regressions and timeouts to see whether a few failures outweigh the wins.

sections.title: Read recent research as testable claims
sections.html:
The arithmetic gives us questions to ask of papers. Lehmann, Sulimov and Stockinger study evaluation of learned optimizers: their comparison depends strongly on how workloads are split, and PostgreSQL wins most tested comparisons. That result concerns those methods and tests; it does not rule out every learned optimizer. GRASP instead predicts cardinalities from query/count observations without raw-table access and studies incomplete or imbalanced join templates. These papers answer different questions.

A query template keeps query structure while replacing changing literal values with placeholders. city='A' and city='B' share city=?; adding AND pass=1 creates another structure. If future work contains unseen joins, holding out only literal values may test the wrong generalization problem.

There is another useful distinction: an accurate guess is not a safe upper bound. In an original join R(k)⋈S(k), counts for keys k1,k2 are R=(3,1) and S=(2,2). The first key makes 3×2=6 pairs; the second makes 1×2=2; total=8. Cauchy–Schwarz gives √(3²+1²)×√(2²+2²)=√80≈8.94, so the integer output is at most 8. A prediction of 7 is close but is not an upper bound.

The Lp-norms paper studies more general join-size bounds. Our two-vector calculation explains the distinction, not its full theorem. Read each guarantee with its assumptions; then ask whether you need a point prediction, a one-sided bound, or a correct lookup.

Sources for this section: Lehmann, Sulimov and Stockinger (PVLDB 2024); GRASP (PVLDB 2025); Join Size Bounds using Lp-Norms on Degree Sequences (PODS 2024). Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: Paper-first experiment: generalization without leakage
sections.html:
We now need an experiment that can expose the failure just described. Fix one Customer snapshot and six count queries: Q1 city='A', Q2 city='B', Q3 city='C'; Q4 city='A' AND pass=1, Q5 city='B' AND pass=1, Q6 city='C' AND pass=1. Q1–Q3 share a template; Q4–Q6 share a second.

For a new-literal test on known templates, train on Q1/Q4, tune choices on Q2/Q5, and reserve Q3/Q6 untouched for the final score. For a new-template test, instead train on Q1, tune on Q2/Q3, and hold all Q4–Q6 out. These are alternative designs. Letting Q4 influence tuning in the second design destroys the unseen-template test. A time-held-out workload needs its date boundary fixed before inspecting results.

Optional implementation can use one table, a CPU regression tool and a small label budget. Record split IDs, observed counts, estimates, q-errors, plans, timings, dataset hash and seed. Compare native estimates, a histogram or simple regression, and the proposed model with equal label budgets. Include collection/training, inference, execution, timeouts and worst regressions.

To learn why the method works, change one thing at a time. Halve labels while holding snapshot, split, model and timing fixed: that is an ablation. Test workload overlap separately. Unsupported SQL, unfamiliar inputs or inference errors require a conventional fallback; confidence is not a correctness proof. GPU training is optional, and a controlled negative result is still useful.

Key takeaway

Evaluate the workload you want to generalize to, not just a convenient random split.

sections.title: Seminar exercise and answer
sections.html:
A report says median q-error is 1.4 and mean execution speedup is 2×. It omits inference, training and three timed-out queries. Before accepting the headline, separate what was measured from what the claim needs.

Write a fair conclusion and a next experiment.

The reported estimation score and execution-only comparison may improve on the selected workload. End-to-end benefit and robustness are not established. First request a timeout-aware workload total and planning/collection/training costs. Then freeze a template-held-out or time-held-out test with comparable baseline tuning. A timeout cannot be removed simply because it lowers the mean. This experiment would distinguish a useful selector from a favorable reporting boundary.

Finish by stating the contract in one sentence: this component makes this decision, on this supported workload, with these checks and fallback. That sentence should be meaningful even to a reader who does not know the model architecture.

quiz.question: A learned selector saves 4 ms of execution but adds 7 ms of planning. What follows?
options: It improves end-to-end latency by 3 ms.
Q-error must be below one.
The query result must be incorrect.
It worsens end-to-end latency by 3 ms, before amortized training cost.
quiz.explanation: Added planning is 7 ms and saved execution is 4 ms, so the total grows by 7−4=3 ms before training is amortized. A legal plan can be slower; this performance change says nothing by itself about SQL result correctness.

questions.question: An estimator predicts 500 rows when the actual positive count is 5,000. What is its q-error?
questions.explanation: Compute both directions: estimate/actual=500/5,000=0.1 and actual/estimate=5,000/500=10. Q-error takes the larger, 10. It is a multiplicative error, not the difference of 4,500 rows, and for positive inputs it cannot be below one.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Why hold complete query templates out of a learned-optimizer test?
options: To avoid measuring query latency.
To test generalization beyond structurally similar training queries.
To ensure all cardinality estimates are exact.
To guarantee the new optimizer wins.
questions.explanation: Queries with different literals can still share a structure, such as city=?. A random split may put that structure in both training and test. Holding complete templates out tests new structure; it neither guarantees correct estimates nor guarantees a win.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A learned index predicts a position. What else is needed for correct lookup?
options: An embedding similarity score.
A verified search/correction procedure and an appropriate bound or fallback.
Only a low average training loss.
A GPU in every case.
questions.explanation: Prediction 420 with a valid error bound 6 narrows a lookup to 414–426; it does not identify the answer without comparing actual keys. A correct enclosing search or fallback must cover prediction errors and updates. Low average training loss alone cannot guarantee that a particular future key is found.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is the difference between a cardinality upper bound and a point estimate?
options: An upper bound must equal the exact count.
An upper bound is intended to never be below the true value under its assumptions; a point estimate need not satisfy that.
A point estimate is always more expensive.
They are identical if the estimate has low mean error.
questions.explanation: An upper bound must stay at or above the true count whenever its assumptions hold. A point estimate can be below or above. In the lesson, true join size 8 is bounded by √80≈8.94, while prediction 7 is close but not an upper bound.

lqo.authors: Claude Lehmann, Pavel Sulimov, Kurt Stockinger
lqo.supports: An end-to-end learned-optimizer evaluation framework; sensitivity to training/test design; PostgreSQL wins in most tested comparisons, depending on split. This is evidence about the evaluated systems and protocol, not impossibility of learned optimization.
